explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The song says, "Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good." The reason comes in the same breath as the call. I once made a whole speech before telling a baker what the dough was for, so I respect a song that gets right to it.

Near is a lovely word, but it isn't the one this verse uses. The song says, "Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good." The reason is His goodness, and it's sitting right there in verse 1. No digging needed, friend.

Patient is a word I could use after some of my slow oven mornings, but it isn't in this verse. The song says, "Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good." Goodness is the reason it gives, and it gives it right away. So the answer was hiding in plain sight, friend.
That's it, friend. The line says, "His loving devotion endures forever." Not a long time, not a really long time. Forever. And the song says it again and again, so you will not forget it.

A lifetime is long, but this song goes further. It says, "His loving devotion endures forever." A lifetime ends, and forever doesn't. The song keeps repeating that line, so the news is even bigger than it first sounds.

A season comes and goes, and the song says nothing like that about His loving devotion. It says, "His loving devotion endures forever." Forever is a lot longer than a season, friend. I can barely make a batch of cookies last through one.
The song doesn't say anything about angels helping here. It says, "He alone does great wonders." Alone is the key word, friend. The great wonders are credited to Him and nobody else.
Right, friend. Verse 4 says, "He alone does great wonders." There's no helper list and no assistants mentioned. When the song says alone, it means alone.

Yes, friend. The song says, "By His insight He made the heavens." Every star up there came from insight, not from a lucky accident. And all of it is followed by that same line about His loving devotion.
It's actually true, friend. Verse 5 says, "By His insight He made the heavens." So the heavens came by insight. I like to think my own cookies come from insight, though some of them come from hope.

That's right, friend. The song says, "He spread out the earth upon the waters." From the heavens it comes down to the ground under our feet. The refrain about His loving devotion follows right behind it.
This one is true, friend. Verse 6 says, "He spread out the earth upon the waters." The earth is spread out, and the song says it was Him. I can barely spread dough on one counter, so I'm impressed.
Yes, friend. The song says He made "the sun to rule the day." The sun has the day shift. It's a very big job, and the sun never calls in sick.
Right. The song says "the moon and stars to govern the night." So the moon and stars take the night. And the bakery is under the same sky, friend.

Seasons is a good guess, but it isn't in these verses. The song says the sun rules the day and the moon and stars govern the night. So each great light gets a job, and seasons aren't the job. The song keeps it simple, friend.

The sea does show up in this song, but not here. Verses 8 and 9 say the sun is to rule the day, and the moon and stars are to govern the night. The sea comes later, when the song gets to the Red Sea. Hang on, friend, we'll get there.

The earth is in the song, but verse 6 handles that one, where He spread it out upon the waters. These verses are about the great lights. The sun rules the day and the moon and stars govern the night. It's a bit like my chocolate chips and sprinkles, friend: each one has its own spot.

Not quiet, friend. The song says He brought Israel out "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm." A mighty hand and an outstretched arm are the opposite of tiptoeing. The song wants us to see His strength.

That's right, friend. Verse 12 says He brought Israel out "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm." That's a power on display, not a sneaking out the back door. I would have tripped over a rolling pin trying to be quiet.

Yes, friend. The song says He "led Israel through the midst." The sea is divided in two, and Israel goes right through the middle of it. The song doesn't say it was an easy walk, only that He led them.

explanations.answer: Keeps them waiting on the shore
explanations.explanation: Waiting on the shore isn't what the song says. Verse 14 says He "led Israel through the midst." Once the sea is divided in two, Israel goes through it. I know waiting well, friend, but this isn't that kind of verse.

explanations.answer: Has them camp beside the water
explanations.explanation: Camping isn't in this song, friend. Verse 14 says He "led Israel through the midst." So Israel goes through the divided sea, not beside it. I'd have set up an oven on the shore, but that's just me.

explanations.answer: They are swept into the sea
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The song says He "swept Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea." Pharaoh was Egypt's king. Israel went through the divided sea, and Pharaoh and his army ended up in it. It's a serious moment, so I'll just let the verse speak.

The song doesn't mention them turning back. Verse 15 says He "swept Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea." Pharaoh was Egypt's king, and he and his army end up in the sea. It's a heavy moment, friend.
Peace isn't what the song describes, friend. Verse 15 says He "swept Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea." Pharaoh was Egypt's king. It's a heavy part of the song, and the verse says it plainly.
Yes, friend. The song says He "gave their land as an inheritance." The kings were Sihon and Og, and their land became a heritage for His servant Israel. Think of it as a gift handed down.
Gold would be shiny, but it isn't what the song says. Verse 21 says He gave their land as an inheritance. The land was the inheritance, friend, and the song names Israel as the one receiving it.

Flocks are a good guess, but the song says land. Verse 21 says He gave their land as an inheritance, and verse 22 calls it a heritage to His servant Israel. So the inheritance was the land itself, friend. I'd have been happy with a cookie jar.
That's it, friend. The song says He "freed us from our enemies." First He remembered us in our low estate, and then He freed us. And the refrain about His loving devotion comes right after.
Debts are a real weight, friend, and I know about bills. But verse 24 names something else. It says He "freed us from our enemies." So the song says enemies, and nothing about money.
Fears feel heavy, I know. But this verse names something different. It says He "freed us from our enemies." So the song says enemies here, friend.
The song says more than that, friend. Verse 25 says, "He gives food to every creature." Every creature is a big group. Nothing in that verse says only His own people.
That's right, friend. The song says, "He gives food to every creature." Every creature, not just some. Even the crumb collectors under my counter are in that group.
Yes, friend. The song opens with "Give thanks to the LORD," and it closes with "Give thanks to the God of heaven!" It ends where it began. And both times, His loving devotion endures forever.

This one is true, friend. Verse 1 says, "Give thanks to the LORD," and verse 26 says, "Give thanks to the God of heaven!" So the song ends with another call to give thanks, the same as it began. It's a nice way to finish, like closing the oven door gently.
